arXiv:2605.20530v1 [cs.AI] 19 May 2026

AgentAtlas: Beyond Outcome Leaderboards for LLM Agents

Parsa Mazaheri Affiliation: University of California, Santa Cruz Email: pmazaher@ucsc.edu    Kasra Mazaheri Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Email: mazaheri@mit.edu
Abstract

Large language model agents now act on codebases, browsers, operating systems, calendars, files, and tool ecosystems, but the benchmarks used to evaluate them are fragmented: each emphasizes a different unit of measurement (final task success, tool-call validity, repeated-pass consistency, trajectory safety, or attack robustness). A line of 2024–2025 work (Kapoor et al., 2024; Kapoor et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2025; Barke et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026) has converged on the diagnosis that a single accuracy column is no longer the right unit of comparison for deployable agents. AgentAtlas extends this line of work with four components: (i) a six-state control-decision taxonomy (Act / Ask / Refuse / Stop / Confirm / Recover); (ii) a nine-category trajectory-failure taxonomy with two orthogonal hierarchical labels (primary_error_source, impact); (iii) a taxonomy-aware vs. taxonomy-blind methodology that measures how much of a model’s apparent capability comes from the supervision in the prompt; and (iv) a benchmark-coverage audit mapping fifteen agent benchmarks against six behavioral axes. To demonstrate the methodology we run a small fixed eight-model set (1,342 generated items, four frontier closed and four open-weight) under both prompt modes. Removing the explicit label menu drops every model’s trajectory accuracy by 14–40 pp to a tight 0.54–0.62 floor regardless of family, and no single model wins on all three of control accuracy, trajectory diagnosis, and tool-context utility retention. We treat the synthetic run as a measurement-protocol demonstration, not a benchmark release.

1 Introduction

Agentic LLMs are no longer only conversational systems. They browse, edit files, call APIs, operate desktop software, interact with user simulators, and orchestrate external tools. This makes the evaluation problem qualitatively different from standard question answering. A chatbot can be judged by the correctness of a final response; an agent must be judged by a sequence of decisions and state changes. The same final answer may be acceptable or unacceptable depending on whether the agent used the right tool, respected user constraints, confirmed sensitive actions, recovered after failed observations, and stopped when the task was complete.

The pace of progress on outcome benchmarks is unusually fast. Between 2023 and early 2026 the best verified success rates on the four canonical outcome benchmarks (OSWorld, WebArena, GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023), WebVoyager (He et al., 2024)) all rose by roughly 5–7×\times (OSWorld team, 2026; web-arena-x, 2026; GAIA benchmark team, 2026; OpenAI, 2025), and five verified OSWorld submissions now sit at or above the 72.4% human baseline. Outcome-only scores are increasingly insufficient and scaffold-sensitive. Newer benchmark families instead expose the evaluation gaps this taxonomy is designed to map: τ\tau-bench reports passk decay and the frontier-model crown flips between k=1k{=}1 and k=4k{=}4 on the 2026 Sierra Overall leaderboard — Opus 4.5 wins pass1 (0.70), Qwen3.5 wins pass4 (0.56) (tau-bench team, 2026; Yao et al., 2024); AgentDojo shows targeted prompt-injection ASR fell from 56.3% on GPT-4-0125 to 7.3% on Claude 3.7 Sonnet while utility-under-attack still trails clean utility by ≈\approx11 pp (AgentDojo team, 2025; Debenedetti et al., 2024); AgentRx localizes critical failure steps in failed trajectories (Microsoft Research, 2026); ATBench evaluates long-horizon trajectory safety (Li et al., 2026); and MCP security benchmarks reveal new tool-poisoning and prompt-injection surfaces (Yang et al., 2025; MCPTox authors, 2025). Anthropic’s computer-use work and the broader Claude Code ecosystem have made agentic coding and GUI interaction a central practical use case (Anthropic, 2024a), and the Model Context Protocol has further accelerated tool-connected assistants (Anthropic, 2024b).

The field therefore has many strong pieces, but not one shared map. A coding benchmark may report a resolved-issue percentage, a browser benchmark may report functional task success, a security benchmark may report attack success rate, and a trajectory benchmark may report critical-step localization. These metrics are not wrong; they are incomplete when used alone. The taxonomy introduced here is designed as a unifying layer over these benchmark families. It asks: what behavior is being measured, what behavior is missing, and which failures would be invisible if we only looked at final task success?

This is a taxonomy and measurement paper. AgentAtlas does not aim to replace existing benchmarks or introduce a new leaderboard; instead, it provides a compact vocabulary for control decisions and trajectory failures, applies that vocabulary to audit existing benchmarks, and demonstrates that prompt format and evaluation axis can change model rankings on a fixed synthetic evaluation set.

A preview of how decisive these axes are: an uncertainty-aware ask-policy on ambiguous SWE-bench Verified tasks lifts overall resolution by 8.2 pp (61.2→69.4%61.2\to 69.4\%) (Fig. D.5); switching τ\tau-bench from pass1 to pass4 reorders the leaderboard (Fig. 2); CCBench moves a Claude-Code deployment 50+ pp by version swap alone (Fig. D.3).

2 AgentAtlas as a Taxonomy and Measurement Study

AgentAtlas is a taxonomy and measurement study for agent evaluation. The taxonomy component defines two behavioral units—control decisions and trajectory failures—that cut across existing agent benchmarks. The measurement component asks how benchmark conclusions change when those units are made explicit: first through a coverage audit of existing benchmarks, and second through a small synthetic demonstration that compares taxonomy-aware and taxonomy-blind prompting.

Central claim.

Final task success is an insufficient unit of measurement for deployable LLM agents. A complete evaluation must separate outcome correctness from control-decision quality and trajectory quality.

Contributions.

The primary contribution is AgentAtlas: a taxonomy and measurement protocol for diagnosing LLM agents beyond final task success. We instantiate it through four components:

  1. 1.

    A six-state control-decision taxonomy (Act / Ask / Refuse / Stop / Confirm / Recover) for tool-using agents.

  2. 2.

    A nine-category trajectory-failure taxonomy linking tool, observation, recovery, and safety failures into a single vocabulary.

  3. 3.

    A benchmark-coverage audit over 15 agent benchmarks across six evaluation axes, showing which behaviors the field already measures and which it does not.

  4. 4.

    A focused empirical demonstration — a generated Control split (684 items), Trajectory split (400 items), and Security split (258 items), totalling 1,342 items — evaluated on a fixed eight-model set (four frontier closed + four open-weight) under both taxonomy-aware and taxonomy-blind prompting (§7). The set is positioned as a measurement-protocol vehicle, not a public benchmark release.

The scope is intentionally narrow enough to be executable. The taxonomy focuses on two core axes: (i) control decisions—whether the agent should act, ask, refuse, stop, confirm, or recover; and (ii) trajectory mistakes—whether the sequence of actions, observations, and tool calls is valid, safe, and efficient. Benchmark checklist coverage, MCP/tool security, and memory/state failures are included as secondary axes because they affect the same behavior. Multi-agent systems are mentioned only where they provide trajectory data, such as Magentic-One traces used by AgentRx, but are not the main target.

Using numbers reported by existing papers is appropriate for the taxonomy and benchmark-audit sections, because the objective is to compare evaluation designs and reported gaps. However, the paper does not treat all reported numbers as a direct model ranking. Different papers use different agents, scaffolds, tools, prompts, timeouts, budgets, and evaluators. For our own empirical section, we run a fixed set of frontier and open models on a controlled generated dataset.

2.1 Position Relative to Concurrent Work

AgentAtlas adds three pieces relative to a line of 2024–2025 multi-axis evaluation work (Kapoor et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2025; Kapoor et al., 2024; Yehudai et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2024; Zhuge et al., 2024): (i) the six-gate control-decision policy that no concurrent work scores as a unified unit, (ii) the taxonomy-aware-vs-blind methodology measuring how much of a model’s apparent capability comes from prompt supervision, and (iii) the fifteen-benchmark coverage audit. Our trajectory taxonomy is adopted from AgentRx with two orthogonal hierarchical extensions (primary_error_source, impact; see §4.2). Detailed positioning relative to HAL, MAST, AAATM, and the Yehudai survey is in Appendix F.

The rest of the paper follows this structure: §3 gives the benchmark background needed for the audit; §4 defines the AgentAtlas taxonomy; §5 motivates the measurement problem with reported results; §6 applies the taxonomy to benchmark coverage; §7 demonstrates the measurement protocol on a fixed synthetic set.

3 Background: Benchmark Families

The current benchmark landscape can be grouped into five families. Coding-agent benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified (SWE-bench team / OpenAI collaboration, 2024), CCBench (CCBench team, 2026)) report outcome metrics on real GitHub-issue resolution or small-codebase tasks.

Web and computer-use benchmarks (WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023), OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024)) evaluate agents in interactive digital environments. Between 2023 and early 2026 the human gap on OSWorld inverted (top-5 runs 73.1–82.6%, at or above the 72.4% human baseline) and on WebArena / GAIA shrank to within 4 pp of human. The dominant confound at this frontier is scaffold sensitivity: agent-s3 w/ GPT-5 moves 65.6 →\to 69.9% on OSWorld just by switching single-shot to best-of-10, and Anthropic’s Claude-Code stack alone spans a 50 pp range on CCBench across four versions (Fig. D.3). Outcome-only scores increasingly measure agent-system engineering rather than the LLM alone.

Tool-use benchmarks cover API and user-tool interaction. API-Bank (Li et al., 2023) ships 73 tools and 314 dialogues; τ\tau-bench reports Pass1–Pass4 to isolate consistency rather than first-attempt success; ToolSandbox (Lu et al., 2024) adds stateful execution, a user simulator, and dynamic milestone evaluation.

Security benchmarks probe adversarial tool / context settings. AgentDojo contains 97 tasks and 629 prompt-injection cases; MCPSecBench identifies 17 attack types across four MCP surfaces; MCPTox evaluates tool poisoning on live MCP servers.

Trajectory-diagnosis benchmarks target the limitation of final-success metrics. AgentRx releases 115 manually annotated failed trajectories with a nine-category taxonomy; ATBench provides 1,000 long-horizon traces balancing safe and unsafe; AgentProcessBench provides 1,000 trajectories with 8,509 step annotations. They focus on trajectory diagnosis rather than a general map of control decisions and benchmark-coverage gaps. §4 introduces the control and trajectory axes, §5 synthesizes existing numbers, and §6 audits which benchmarks measure which axis.

A compact reference card listing each benchmark’s primary unit, current top score, and primary axis is in Appendix A (Table A.2).

4 AgentAtlas Taxonomy

4.1 Control-Decision Axis

The control-decision axis is the main new organizing vocabulary. Many existing benchmarks imply these behaviors but do not score them explicitly. To our knowledge no prior work formalizes this six-gate decomposition as a single decision-policy taxonomy; per-gate prior art and the relation to HAL, MAST, AgentRx, and AgentDojo is summarized in Appendix F.

We define six primary control states:

  • •

    Act — task is sufficiently specified, authorized, and safe to execute.

  • •

    Ask — task is materially underspecified; progressing without clarification would likely cause a wrong or unsafe action.

  • •

    Refuse — action is disallowed, harmful, or beyond acceptable authority.

  • •

    Stop — agent has reached task completion, determined impossibility, or detected that further action is redundant or unsafe.

  • •

    Confirm — task is feasible but sensitive or irreversible and therefore requires explicit user sign-off.

  • •

    Recover — current trajectory has failed and the correct next step is repair, rollback, re-grounding, or re-planning rather than blind continuation.

Ask-vs-Assume behavior is directly measurable: the Ask or Assume? study (Ask or Assume team, 2026) on an under-specified SWE-bench Verified subset shows an uncertainty-aware multi-agent scaffold lifting overall task resolution from 61.2% to 69.4% (8.2 pp gain) by asking selectively when its own uncertainty signal flags the request as ambiguous (Fig. D.5, Appendix D).

4.2 Trajectory-Failure Axis

Trajectory failures are where final-answer evaluation becomes most misleading. An agent may reach a correct state through an unsafe path, or fail because of an early recoverable error that propagates. AgentRx makes this point directly by localizing the first unrecoverable step in failed trajectories and providing a nine-category failure taxonomy. AgentProcessBench similarly argues that tool-use failures often have irreversible side effects and therefore require step-level verification. ATBench extends this perspective to long-horizon safety, where risk may be planted early and realized later.

We adopt AgentRx’s nine-category taxonomy rather than proposing a new one. The nine categories below are AgentRx’s labels with minor terminology updates for consistency with the control axis (e.g., we use “Recovery failure” rather than AgentRx’s “fails to recover from observation”). The single-label assignment is unchanged.

  1. 1.

    Goal misinterpretation — agent works on the wrong problem or misreads a constraint.

  2. 2.

    Wrong tool selection — inappropriate tool or action modality.

  3. 3.

    Wrong argument / wrong target — correct tool, incorrect ID / path / parameter.

  4. 4.

    Observation failure — misreads UI state, tool output, or external evidence.

  5. 5.

    Constraint violation — policy, permission, or user constraint broken during execution.

  6. 6.

    Recovery failure — agent does not respond appropriately to a prior mistake.

  7. 7.

    Looping or over-action — continues past a reasonable stopping point.

  8. 8.

    Unsafe trust of external content — malicious or untrusted tool output hijacks the trajectory.

  9. 9.

    State or memory contamination — stale or contaminated context distorts later decisions.

Our extension is two orthogonal hierarchical labels that decompose what AgentRx treats as a single label, designed to make the trajectory split easier to slice for diagnosis: a primary_error_source field (wrong_tool / wrong_argument / missed_constraint / observation_misread / failure_to_recover / valid) that names the kind of mistake, and an impact field (unsafe_side_effect / privacy_leak / wrong_final_state / unnecessary_cost / no_impact) that names the consequence. The two are independent — the same kind of mistake can have different impacts depending on context — and our §7 evaluation reports per-axis accuracy on each (primary_src_acc, impact_acc, joint pri+impact). AgentRx and AgentProcessBench do not separate these two layers; we propose this decomposition as a small extension rather than a replacement of their taxonomy.

4.3 Secondary Axes: Security, Memory, and Efficiency

Three secondary axes complete the taxonomy: security (tool-context isolation under adversarial inputs), memory & state (cross-session contamination, stale context), and efficiency (excessive steps, cost, or latency hidden by pass@1). The §6 audit assigns no benchmark a strong-coverage score on efficiency; the OSWorld-Human re-analysis (OSWorld-Human team, 2025) reports the best OSWorld agent at 42.5% under standard scoring vs. 17.4% under a stricter grouped-action efficiency metric, with leading agents taking 1.4–2.7×\times more steps than the human-minimum path (Fig. D.2 in Appendix D). Detailed motivation for each secondary axis — MCPSecBench, MCPTox, ToolSandbox state, planning-vs-action latency split — is in Appendix E.

5 Motivating Evidence from Existing Results

Outcome leaderboards are rapidly improving and increasingly scaffold-sensitive. Recent submissions have sharply narrowed the human gap on OSWorld, WebArena, and GAIA, with OSWorld now reporting several above-human system submissions; however, these numbers increasingly reflect agent-system scaffolds, retry budgets, and best-of-N voting at least as much as base-model capability — agent-s3 w/ GPT-5 moves from 65.6 →\to 69.9% on OSWorld just by switching single-shot to best-of-10. The same pattern shows in coding: CCBench’s Claude-Code submissions span Haiku 4.5 (21.9%) →\to Opus 4.6 (72.7%), a 50.8 pp range driven by version + scaffold interaction within a single provider. Full progression timelines for OSWorld and CCBench are in Appendix D (Figs. D.4 and D.3).

τ\tau-bench is the strongest external evidence that single-shot success is insufficient (Fig. 2). On the May-2026 Sierra Overall leaderboard, Claude Opus 4.5 wins pass1 (0.70) but Qwen3.5-397B-A17B wins pass4 (0.56) — rank-3 becomes rank-1 as kk grows because Qwen has the flattest decay curve (−-12 pp vs. ≈\approx−-18 pp). Even the strongest 2026 system loses ≈\approx25 pp between pass1 and pass4 on Retail (Qwen 0.84 →\to 0.60). The one controlled pair on the leaderboard — GPT-5.2 with reasoning on vs. off — gains 14 pp on Retail pass1 but 23 pp on pass4: reasoning moves consistency more than it moves single-shot correctness. A pass1-only ranking would ship a different agent than a pass4-aware ranking.

Security and trajectory diagnostics tell the same story on different axes. AgentDojo’s targeted prompt-injection ASR has fallen from 56.3% on GPT-4-0125 (2024) to 7.3% on Claude 3.7 Sonnet (2025-02) — an order-of-magnitude reduction — but utility-under-attack still trails clean utility by ≈\approx11 pp on the same model, so prompt injection is partially mitigable but not cost-free. AgentRx reports +23.6 pp gains in failure localization over prompting baselines on 115 manually annotated failed trajectories, and AgentProcessBench adds 8,509 step annotations at 89.1% inter-annotator agreement. These are exactly the axes where a single outcome metric is silent.

6 Applying AgentAtlas to Benchmark Coverage

The audit scores each benchmark on a simple 0/1/2 scale across six evaluation axes, using this rubric:

  • •

    0 (absent): the benchmark does not directly test or report the axis.

  • •

    1 (partial): the benchmark implicitly exercises the axis but does not isolate it.

  • •

    2 (strong): the benchmark directly scores or annotates the axis.

The 15 audited benchmarks are: WebArena, OSWorld, OSWorld-Human, WebVoyager, GAIA, AssistantBench, SWE-bench Verified, CCBench, τ\tau-bench, ToolSandbox, API-Bank, Ask-or-Assume?, AgentDojo, AgentRx, AgentProcessBench. Fig. 3 then aggregates the 15 audited benchmarks per axis to show which behaviors the field already covers and which it does not. The purpose is not to criticize individual benchmarks — each was designed for a specific goal — but to show which behaviors remain under-measured when the field is viewed as a whole.

The main gap is not that benchmarks ignore agents; it is that each benchmark isolates one slice of agent behavior. SWE-bench Verified tests whether a patch resolves an issue, but not whether the agent asked when the issue was ambiguous or stopped after a minimal correct fix. WebArena and OSWorld test realistic interaction, but failure attribution is limited relative to trace-level datasets. τ\tau-bench and ToolSandbox provide stronger tool/user/state interactions, but their reported metrics are not a general failure taxonomy. AgentDojo and MCP security benchmarks stress adversarial tool settings but do not cover ordinary under-specification. AgentRx, ATBench, and AgentProcessBench finally provide rich trajectory labels, but they do not replace outcome benchmarks or benign control-decision evaluation.

7 Measurement Demonstration: Prompt-Format and Axis Sensitivity

This section demonstrates the §4 taxonomy and §6 audit on a small fixed evaluation, treated as a measurement-protocol demonstration rather than a public benchmark release (caveats in §8). The aim is to show that two methodology choices — prompt format (taxonomy-aware vs. blind) and evaluation axis (control vs. trajectory vs. tool-context utility) — change the apparent ranking of the same eight models on the same items. This is the contribution that no benchmark in the §6 audit currently surfaces.

7.1 Dataset and Prompt Modes

The evaluation set has three splits totalling 1,342 items, all generated by Claude Opus 4.7 with Pydantic schema validation, dedupe, and a license-leakage probe:

  • •

    Control — 684 short task states labeled by the correct decision across the six gates (Act / Ask / Refuse / Stop / Confirm / Recover), drawn from six practical domains (email/calendar, files/documents, coding, customer support, web forms, MCP-like tools). The label mix is intentionally weighted toward Confirm and Recover because irreversible-action evaluation is the hardest published gap.

  • •

    Trajectory — 400 short traces spanning the nine trajectory failure categories from §4.2 (wrong tool, wrong arguments, missed constraint, observation misread, recovery failure, looping/over-action, unsafe trust of external content, state/memory contamination, plus a valid no-failure label), each annotated with the two orthogonal hierarchical labels primary_error_source and impact.

  • •

    Security — 258 items targeting tool-context isolation under poisoned tool outputs and related adversarial contexts (malicious documents, hijacked tool responses, attacker-controlled email/web content).

Each item is presented to the evaluator under two prompt modes:

  • •

    Taxonomy-aware — the prompt names the closed-set label menu (the six control gates, or the nine trajectory categories, or the security action set) and asks the model to pick one with a short justification.

  • •

    Taxonomy-blind — the prompt removes the label menu and asks the model to produce a free-form natural-language diagnosis. A deterministic substring rule then maps the free-form output back to the same closed set; unmatched outputs fall back to a single Haiku-4.5 mapper call (“which of these labels best fits this verdict?”).

The dataset-generation pipeline (seed catalogue, prompt clauses, schema, dedupe, license audit, batch worker design) is described in Appendix B.

7.2 Models and Metrics

The eight evaluators are four frontier closed (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, gpt-5.4-mini, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) and four open-weight (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, Ministral-3-14B-Instruct-2512, gpt-oss-20B). Open models were served via local vLLM. Each (model ×\times split ×\times prompt-mode) cell is one run; the full sweep is 8 ×\times 3 ×\times 2 = 48 runs and ≈\approx21,000 per-item judgments. Full per-(model ×\times split ×\times prompt-mode) tables are in Appendix C; a compact axis-by-axis reference is given by Table F.1 (Appendix F). The three headline findings are:

  • •

    Control: aware-mode accuracy clusters within 7 pp across seven of eight models (0.87–0.95); the explicit label menu alone makes models look similar.

  • •

    Trajectory: removing the nine-category menu drops every model 14–40 pp; the blind-mode floor compresses to 0.54–0.62 regardless of family.

  • •

    Tool-context utility: model rankings invert across axes — the model that tops control (Haiku 4.5) is the weakest frontier model on tool-context utility (0.28); the model that tops tool-context utility (gpt-5.4-mini) is the weakest frontier model on trajectory.

7.3 Results: Taxonomy Aware vs. Blind

Under taxonomy-aware control prompting the eight models cluster within 7 pp (0.870–0.946 for the seven competitive models; gpt-oss-20B at 0.743 trails the pack). Trajectory aware accuracy spans an even narrower 0.69–0.95 range. Open Gemma-4-26B-A4B (0.943 trajectory aware) outranks frontier Sonnet 4.6 (0.885) and gpt-5.4-mini (0.818); Qwen3.6-35B-A3B trails Sonnet by under 5 pp on control. A single-number ranking on either taxonomy-aware split would not differentiate these eight models in any deployment-relevant way — exactly the §3 critique of OSWorld / WebArena rankings, replicated on our own data.

Removing the explicit taxonomy from the prompt drops every model 14–40 pp on trajectory diagnosis (Fig. D.1 in Appendix D). Per-model drops range from −-14.8 pp (gpt-oss-20B) to −-40.1 pp (Gemma-4-26B-A4B), with frontier-vs-open family means within one point (−-30.5 vs −-31.4 pp); the full per-model breakdown is in Appendix C (Table C.2). The smallest drop is on an open-weight model and the largest is also on an open-weight model, so the contrast is not cleanly explained by a frontier-vs-open robustness gap. What does separate cleanly is the blind-mode floor: every model’s blind accuracy lands in an 8-point band (0.54–0.62), independent of whether it scored 0.69 or 0.95 in aware mode. Once the explicit label menu is removed, the eight models become roughly indistinguishable on trajectory diagnosis — the strongest empirical support in the paper for the thesis that a single coarse-label aware-mode metric measures supervision more than capability.

7.4 Results: Cross-Axis Incoherence

No model wins all three axes (Fig. 4). Per-model radar profiles reveal sharp asymmetries that a tier-aggregated leaderboard hides. Haiku 4.5 dominates control (0.95) and trajectory (0.95) but is the weakest frontier model on tool-context utility retention (0.28) — it refuses 68% of benign tasks under aware mode and 84% under blind. gpt-5.4-mini inverts the pattern: it tops tool-context utility (0.98) but is mid-pack on control (0.91) and last among frontier on trajectory (0.82). Open Gemma-4-26B-A4B has the strongest maximin profile in the set — its worst axis is 0.87 (control), better than every other model’s worst-axis score (Sonnet 0.79, gpt-5.4-mini 0.82, Gemini 0.70, gpt-oss 0.69, Qwen 0.40, Haiku 0.28, Ministral 0.08). Gemma is not top-half on every individual axis (it sits 6th of 8 on control); it is the only model that avoids a sharp asymmetry across the three axes. The practical implication: a deployment team that picks by a single axis will end up with a model that is among the worst in the set on the axis they did not optimize. This replicates the τ\tau-bench Pass1-vs-Pass4 rank flip within our own evaluation.

8 Limitations

Several broad limitations apply to the synthesized landscape. Reported results from different papers are not directly comparable because scaffolds, prompts, budgets, tools, and data conditions differ; rapidly changing leaderboards may go stale, so the paper focuses on robust benchmark properties rather than leaderboard-chasing; generated control-decision data may over-simplify production environments unless validated against real tool traces; security benchmarks are version-sensitive because MCP servers, clients, and provider policies evolve quickly; and trajectory annotation is subjective unless labels are carefully defined and at least a subset is human-reviewed. In particular, OSWorld’s public leaderboard mixes bare-model runs, tool-augmented scaffolds, and best-of-N voting; our quoted numbers do not normalize for inference-compute budget. Best-of-N submissions inflate the observed score with an order of magnitude more test-time compute than the same base model under single-shot — so leaderboard positions should not be read as pure-model rankings.

Five further caveats apply specifically to the §7 empirical results. (i) Generator-locked. The 1,342-item dataset and all gold labels were produced by a single Claude Opus 4.7 checkpoint, so “model X agrees with the gold” is conflated with “model X agrees with Opus’s preferences”; our headline aware-mode trajectory ordering plausibly reflects label-style overlap rather than diagnostic capability. (ii) No human-validated calibration subset. Absolute accuracy numbers in §7 are not directly comparable to HAL, MAST, or AgentRx, which anchor on human annotations. (iii) Small support in some Security cells (n=3n=3 refuse-gold, n=7n=7 stop-gold), so the security discussion in §7.4 leans on stable cells (benign_utility_retention at n=192n=192 act-gold, over_refusal_rate) rather than per-label F1. (iv) Mapper accuracy assumed, not measured. We estimate ≈\approx3–5% of blind-mode predictions are routed to a wrong label by the substring + Haiku-fallback rule, so the 14–40 pp drop could be inflated by a few points; the cross-axis incoherence finding (Fig. 4) is unaffected because it uses aware-mode metrics only. (v) Step-boundary ambiguity. Critical-step exact accuracy (0.09–0.15) is treated as exploratory pending a definitional audit; the very large exact-vs-±\pm1 gap (etiology in Appendix B) is consistent with a labeling-convention mismatch rather than a uniform localization failure. The natural follow-ups — multi-generator regen, 100-item mapper audit, step-boundary audit — are the next required steps before §7 is treated as more than a measurement-protocol demonstration.

9 Conclusion

The next stage of agent evaluation should move beyond final success rates. AgentAtlas does not propose a new universal score; it offers a vocabulary for asking which agent behavior a score actually reflects. We unify fragmented benchmarks into a taxonomy of control decisions and trajectory failures, audit fifteen benchmarks against six axes, and demonstrate on a fixed eight-model evaluation that prompt format and evaluation axis change apparent rankings. Outcome-only scores are increasingly insufficient and scaffold-sensitive: the central question is no longer just whether an agent succeeds, but whether it acts, asks, refuses, stops, confirms, and recovers at the right moments. The taxonomy complements rather than replaces existing benchmarks; future evaluations can use it as a checklist across tool choice, argument correctness, ambiguity, refusal calibration, stopping, recovery, state/memory, prompt injection, and cost/latency.

Appendix A Benchmark Coverage Audit — Rubric and Matrix

We score each of the 15 audited benchmarks on a 0/1/2 scale across six evaluation axes. The aggregated bar chart is Fig. 3 in §6; the underlying per-benchmark matrix is reproduced in Table A.1.

Rubric.

  • •

    0 (absent): the benchmark does not directly test or report the axis.

  • •

    1 (partial): the benchmark implicitly exercises the axis (its tasks may require it) but does not isolate or score it.

  • •

    2 (strong): the benchmark directly scores or annotates the axis.

A few patterns are worth highlighting. Tool execution is the only axis with broad strong coverage (9 of 15 benchmarks at 2). Control sits mostly at level 1; only τ\tau-bench and ToolSandbox reach 2. Trajectory diagnosis reaches 2 only in the three dedicated trajectory works (AgentRx, ATBench, AgentProcessBench). Memory & state has just one strong benchmark (ToolSandbox). Efficiency has no benchmark scoring 2 across the audit — exactly the gap §4.3 (and the OSWorld-Human latency analysis in Fig. D.2) is designed to surface.

A.1 Compact benchmark reference

Table A.2 lists ten benchmarks as a quick-look reference card across the five evaluation axes (outcome, control, trajectory, security, efficiency). Each row shows the benchmark’s primary unit of measurement, the headline 2024→\to2026 score with the current top-system attribution, and the axis it most strongly probes. Benchmarks cited only in prose are omitted for brevity.

Appendix B Dataset Generation Pipeline

The 1,342-item synthetic set summarized in §7.1 was built by a single-purpose pipeline that exists alongside the eval harness. This appendix documents the generator, prompts, and validation passes.

Generator and provider. All items and gold labels were produced by Claude Opus 4.7 via the Anthropic Messages API, using OIDC bearer-token auth with a project token to route against a project quota. The pipeline runs as a parallel batch dispatcher (process pool, default concurrency 10 for Anthropic) with tenacity retry + JWT-exp token refresh per worker.

Schema and prompts. Items are validated against per-split JSON schemas for Control, Trajectory, and Security. Each schema defines the closed-set gold label, structured context fields (user instruction, tools, state, ambiguity, hidden risk), and an Opus-validated explanation. Prompts inject the JSON schema into the system message, plus a per-cell seed catalogue: AST-extracted tool / argument / domain names from the τ\tau-bench, AgentDojo, and ToolSandbox source code, sampled at runtime to avoid both repetition and license leakage.

Validation and dedupe. Generated items pass through two post-processing stages. First, a two-judge keep / revise / discard pass (Opus 4.7 generator + a smaller verifier) flags items that are off-spec, leak benchmark text verbatim, or contain inconsistent gold labels. Second, a token-Jaccard near-duplicate filter removes items whose 5-gram overlap exceeds 0.7 with any earlier accepted item in the same split. After both passes, the final counts are 684 / 400 / 258 across Control / Trajectory / Security.

Per-axis design intent.

  • •

    Control — six gates ×\times six domains, intentionally weighted toward Confirm and Recover because evaluating irreversible actions is the hardest published gap.

  • •

    Trajectory — nine categories from AgentRx plus the two orthogonal hierarchical labels primary_error_source and impact. Each category has at least 30 items so per-label F1 is reportable.

  • •

    Security — items target tool-context isolation under poisoned tool outputs, malicious documents, and attacker-controlled email/web content. The gold action set extends Control’s six gates with an explicit act-on-attack failure mode used to compute attack_following_rate.

Limitations. All items and labels are produced by one model family; this is the dominant caveat (§8, caveat (i)). We did not collect a human-validated calibration subset (caveat (ii)). The mapper that converts taxonomy-blind free-form outputs back to closed-set labels is a deterministic substring rule with a Haiku-4.5 fallback for unmatched cases; we estimate ≈\approx3–5% of blind outputs get routed to a wrong label (caveat (iv)).

Etiology of the exact-vs-±\pm1 step gap. The trajectory split also carries a per-trace “critical step” index. Across all eight evaluators we observe exact-step accuracy of 0.09–0.15 but ±\pm1 accuracy of 0.77–0.94 (§8). The very large gap between exact and ±\pm1 is the diagnostic signature of a step-boundary ambiguity — e.g., 0-vs-1 indexing, or a definition gap where models point to the tool-call step while the gold points to the following observation/action step — rather than a uniform failure of step localization. We therefore treat the exact-step number as exploratory pending a step-boundary audit.

Appendix C Full Per-Model Results

Tables C.1–C.4 reproduce the per-(model ×\times split ×\times prompt-mode) results that §7 references.

The cross-tier security row is the most striking: blind-mode utility retention rises for open models in the mean because under-prompted open evaluators default to acting more often (Ministral 0.078 →\to 0.578) — i.e., the blind prompt removes their cautious refusal heuristic. We do not interpret this as “open models are safer under blind mode”; it is an artefact of how each family responds to under-specification, and re-enforces caveat (iv) (mapper accuracy unvalidated).

Appendix D Additional Figures

Appendix E Secondary Evaluation Axes

§4.3 pointed to this appendix for the full discussion of the three secondary axes that complete the AgentAtlas taxonomy.

Security. Tool-connected agents introduce new trust boundaries. MCP makes tool integration easier, but tool metadata and tool results can also become adversarial inputs. MCPSecBench identifies MCP attack types across user, client, transport, and server surfaces. MCPTox shows that real MCP servers and authentic tools can be used to construct tool-poisoning tests with high attack success and low refusal rates. These findings fit naturally into the taxonomy as tool-trust and unsafe-delegation trajectory failures.

Memory and state. ToolSandbox is the main benchmark in this draft for stateful conversational tool use, because it tests implicit state dependencies and on-policy conversational evaluation. Long-lived memory across sessions is not the paper’s core experiment because it would expand scope, but state contamination and stale memory appear in the generated-data plan as one of the trajectory categories.

Efficiency. pass@1 can hide excessive steps, cost, or latency. Efficiency is the clearest example of a deployment axis that appears in the literature but is rarely scored strongly: the §6 audit assigns no benchmark a strong-coverage score on this axis. The OSWorld-Human re-analysis shows even the best OSWorld agent achieves 42.5% under standard scoring but only 17.4% under a stricter grouped-action efficiency metric, with leading agents taking roughly 1.4–2.7×\times more steps than the human-minimum path. Fig. D.2 breaks down where that extra wall-clock time goes: across ten applications, planning and reflection together consume 75–95% of agent wall-clock time while pure tool action accounts for under 3%. The strongest case that “efficiency” for agents is primarily a deliberation-cost problem, not an I/O problem.

Appendix F Supplementary Positioning and Results Summary

F.1 Position relative to concurrent work — detailed

§2.1 kept just the contribution-trio summary. The full positioning relative to each cited line of work was: “The ‘go beyond single-number outcome metrics’ position is not new. A line of 2024–2025 papers — AAATM, HAL, MAST, Agent-as-a-Judge, the Yehudai survey, and AgentBoard — has converged on the same diagnosis, each partitioning the multi-axis problem differently: by cost ×\times accuracy ×\times scaffold (HAL), by multi-agent failure modes (MAST, κ=0.88\kappa=0.88 over 1,600 traces), by developer-vs-practitioner methodology (AAATM), or descriptively (Yehudai). None isolates a single-agent control-decision policy as a first-class unit. What this paper adds is three pieces. First, a six-gate control-decision taxonomy (Act / Ask / Refuse / Stop / Confirm / Recover) that no concurrent work scores as a unified policy. Second, a taxonomy-aware vs. taxonomy-blind methodology that measures how much of a model’s apparent capability comes from the supervision in the prompt. Third, an explicit benchmark-coverage audit mapping fifteen benchmarks against six behavioral axes.”

F.2 Six-gate taxonomy — per-gate prior-art prelude

§4.1 opens with a one-sentence statement that the six-gate decomposition is novel; the per-gate prior-art survey it replaced was: “OpenAI’s CUA report, for example, states that CUA asks for confirmation for sensitive actions such as login details or CAPTCHA responses. τ\tau-bench implicitly tests whether the agent can act consistently in tool-user domains. ToolSandbox tests state dependencies and insufficient-information scenarios. AgentDojo and MCP security benchmarks test refusal and unsafe tool-use behavior under attacks. We make these implicit decisions explicit. To our knowledge, the six-gate Act / Ask / Refuse / Stop / Confirm / Recover decomposition is not present as a single decision-policy taxonomy in the concurrent multi-axis evaluation work surveyed in §2.1: HAL scores cost ×\times accuracy ×\times scaffold but does not isolate decision policy; MAST enumerates 14 multi-agent failure modes but does not partition single-agent control decisions; AgentRx focuses on trajectory-level failure localization rather than the per-step decision question. Individual gates have prior names — Confirm appears in OpenAI’s CUA discussion, Refuse is the central concept in AgentDojo, Ask is studied in Ask or Assume?, Stop and Recover surface in AgentProcessBench’s step-level annotations — but the unification into a six-state policy with per-gate evaluation hooks is, as far as we can find, the contribution this paper adds to the concurrent literature.”
